title: What Cheniere Does: One Reportable Segment, Integrated LNG Delivery

epigraph.quote: We have determined that we operate as a single operating and reportable segment.
epigraph.author: Cheniere Energy, 2025 Form 10-K [2]

web_blocks.text: The most important segment fact is the one companies sometimes bury beneath a list of facilities: Cheniere reports one operating and reportable segment. Its CEO receives consolidated operating and financial information, and the company describes its activities as an integrated LNG service. Sabine Pass, Corpus Christi, their connected pipelines, commercial marketing, and delivery support are not separately reported business segments. Do not divide company revenue or operating profit across these physical assets as if Cheniere disclosed a plant-by-plant profit statement; it does not. [2]

The operating segment combines several linked tasks. Cheniere and affiliates acquire natural gas, secure pipeline transportation, liquefy the feed gas, store LNG, load cargoes and sell LNG under long-term sale and purchase agreements, Integrated Production Marketing agreements, or short-, medium- and long-term marketing arrangements. Some cargoes are sold free-on-board at the terminal; for delivered sales, Cheniere arranges shipping and delivery to a receiving terminal. These are activities in one integrated business, not evidence of separately disclosed revenue segments. [2][3]

web_blocks.takeaway: The infrastructure map is useful for understanding operations; it is not a substitute for segment reporting. [2][12]

web_blocks.title: Two terminals, a single operating system

web_blocks.text: Sabine Pass in Cameron Parish, Louisiana has six operating trains, approximately 30 mtpa of production capacity, more than 4.7 Bcf/d of gas-processing capability, five storage tanks, three marine berths and multiple pipeline connections. Its network gives the facility access to gas supplies from a broad set of continental regions east of the Rocky Mountains. Corpus Christi in Texas has ten operating trains after completion of Stage 3, more than 25 mtpa of nominal production capacity, two docks, three storage tanks and pipeline access to supplies including the Permian Basin. Facility scale and physical access are part of the operating advantage, but disclosed site capacity is not a revenue or profit split. [4][5][6][10]

A third-party estimate would still be needed to assign a current revenue share to either facility. Cheniere's consolidated external-customer revenue includes LNG sales and other activity, while the filing's segment note says management evaluates a single integrated business. The same caution applies to the marketing affiliate. It can sell uncontracted production, purchase third-party LNG and market it onward; that is a commercial channel within the segment, not a separately reported profit pool. [2]

web_blocks.title: A customer journey: Petrobras and a free-on-board SPA

web_blocks.text: Petrobras provides a concrete example of the only reported segment's output. Cheniere Marketing, LLC signed an agreement under which Petrobras will purchase approximately 0.8 million tonnes of LNG per year on a free-on-board basis for 22 years. Neither the Cheniere announcement nor Petrobras's release discloses the contract's price, so no per-unit charge should be attached to this example. The general long-term SPA architecture disclosed in the 10-K includes a fixed fee on contracted volume and a variable component, but the precise Petrobras formula is unavailable and should not be inferred from other contracts. Petrobras says long-term volumes are intended to reduce exposure to short-term LNG-market volatility, strengthen gas-portfolio risk management and improve flexibility and security in serving its contracts. Petrobras operates a regasification terminal at Guanabara Bay in Rio de Janeiro, a relevant receiving point for the customer's downstream system. [2][3][13]

The route from resource to buyer begins with Cheniere Marketing's commercial agreement and Cheniere's gas procurement from U.S. producers. Firm transportation moves feed gas through pipeline networks to a liquefaction site. Gas treatment and the refrigeration process cool the gas to liquid form, reducing its volume to roughly one-six-hundredth of its gaseous volume. Storage tanks hold the LNG between production and loading. Cheniere schedules a cargo at the terminal and loads a vessel. Under FOB terms, Petrobras takes delivery at the export terminal and arranges the vessel and the ocean voyage; Petrobras then manages transport to its import terminal and regasification system. The resulting gas can be integrated into its wider supply portfolio. Each stage depends on specifications, vessel scheduling, export authorizations and receiving capacity. [2][3][4][5][13]

The commercial distinction is important. In a delivered-at-place sale, Cheniere arranges chartering and delivery to one or more designated terminals. That shifts vessel procurement and voyage execution toward Cheniere and the accounting transfer point follows the contract's delivery conditions. With FOB, the buyer arranges transport after loading and retains destination flexibility subject to law and the agreement. Petrobras's SPA is explicitly FOB; its contract price is not publicly disclosed in the announcement. [2][3]

web_blocks.title: Do not turn facilities into fictional segments
paragraphs: You can learn a great deal about the two terminals from their capacities, tanks, docks and gas networks. You cannot infer a facility's revenue share, segment margin or stand-alone profit from those operating facts. Cheniere's audited filing explicitly presents one operating and reportable segment; absent a reported allocation, any exact split would be invented. [2][4][5]

web_blocks.text: The group structure explains why segment profit and economic ownership are not identical. Cheniere consolidates Cheniere Partners, which owns the Sabine Pass liquefaction business. At year-end 2025, the parent owned 100% of the general partner and 48.6% of the limited-partner interests, together with incentive distribution rights. Consolidation places the controlled subsidiary's revenues and expenses into group statements; noncontrolling interests then identify the earnings and equity attributable to outside owners. Treating all consolidated profit as if it belonged to the parent would overstate the economics available to Cheniere shareholders. [2]

The filing does disclose revenue by customer geography, based on the principal place of business of the counterparty, but geography does not identify where a cargo was produced or which facility earned a margin. The customer-location table therefore answers a different question from segment reporting. A cargo can originate at Sabine Pass, be sold through a marketing affiliate to a counterparty in one jurisdiction, and eventually reach a receiving terminal elsewhere. The source's accounting geography follows the agreement counterparty, not an operational profit center. [2]

Keep nameplate capacity separate from sold volume. CCL's ten trains and more than 25 mtpa are operating-site capacity facts after Stage 3; the EIA described the project in Bcf/d terms and distinguished nominal capacity from peak capacity. A company can load fewer tonnes than nominal capacity because of commissioning, planned maintenance, weather, operating performance, pipeline supply or cargo schedules. For the same reason, the reported 2026 cargo and TBtu totals are throughput indicators, not an allocation of revenue among trains. [3][5][6]

The Petrobras deal also illustrates the difference between a commercial product and an inferred price. The buyer is Petrobras, not a retail customer; the product is LNG, not an open-ended terminal reservation; the disclosed obligation is approximately 0.8 mtpa FOB for 22 years. Petrobras identifies portfolio flexibility and lower dependence on short-term LNG purchases as the reason for buying long-term volumes. Cheniere's platform supplies the gas chain through procurement, pipeline access and liquefaction, but the 2026 announcement does not disclose the term's index, fixed fee or total value. The company's generic SPA description cannot be used to reverse-engineer Petrobras's exact confidential pricing formula. [2][3][13]

One segment does not mean the financial statements lack detail. The 2026 third-quarter release separately reported LNG revenue, regasification revenue and other revenue. Those categories help describe what customers paid for during that quarter, but they do not disclose operating profit by product, terminal or sales channel. The filing does not tell us what net income, EBITDA or free cash flow each revenue category produced. [2][3]

The go-to-market model is built around negotiated commercial relationships rather than a downstream reseller network. Cheniere Marketing markets available volumes directly through SPAs and shorter-term sales, while the terminal subsidiaries perform liquefaction services and coordinate operational delivery. If the company buys third-party LNG, its marketing affiliate can place those molecules into the broader portfolio. The channel is specialized and institutional, so credit evaluation, destination terms, cargo windows and shipping choices replace broad retail acquisition metrics. [2][3]

The October 2026 QatarEnergy agreements show another form of customer acquisition: long-dated offtake used to underpin future brownfield capacity. SPL and CCL signed agreements for up to 4 mtpa on an FOB basis, beginning in the early 2030s and running through 2054; 1 mtpa depends on an SPL Expansion FID and other conditions. The 2026 Q3 release does not publish the contract prices. This is evidence that Cheniere is extending the commercial book, not a new reportable segment and not an operating-capacity addition today. [3]

The 2025 segment disclosure also defines the profit boundary. The CEO is the CODM, the executive team is organized by function rather than by facility, and financial and operating information is assessed on a single basis consistent with the integrated offering. Net income attributable to Cheniere is the profit measure most consistent with GAAP that the CODM regularly receives. It is therefore inappropriate to reverse-allocate that number across trains using capacity as a proxy. [2]

The company also gives a consolidated customer-concentration test: no external customer accounted for 10% or more of 2025 revenue from contracts with external customers. That is meaningful evidence about annual revenue dependence, but it is not a count of SPAs or a facility mix. The filing separately says customer balances can be more concentrated in receivables and contract assets. Revenue diversity describes who bought during the period; it does not show where the cargo was produced or whether every receivable is equally collectible. [2]

Read the segment note as a description of what management monitors, not as a claim that the operation is simple. The CODM reviews consolidated results, total assets and significant cost categories while making resource-allocation decisions. Train-level engineering data and capacity tables remain useful for assessing execution, but the filing does not transform them into standalone segment accounts. For a reader, the right synthesis is one integrated LNG segment, product revenue categories where reported, one GAAP profit measure and no published profit allocation among Sabine Pass, Corpus Christi and marketing. [2][3]

book_paragraphs: Imagine you are looking at an LNG tanker leaving the Texas or Louisiana coast. It is tempting to call the liquefaction plant the business and stop there. The filing asks you to think more broadly: Cheniere reports one operating and reportable segment. Its leadership reviews the platform on a consolidated basis. Gas sourcing, pipelines, liquefaction, storage, loading, marketing and, on delivered contracts, vessel arrangements all join together to produce a single commercial outcome. [2]

That distinction matters when you try to understand mix. Sabine Pass is a large physical asset with six trains and roughly 30 million tonnes per year of capacity. Corpus Christi now has ten operating trains and more than 25 million tonnes per year of nominal capacity. But those facts do not tell you what proportion of Cheniere's audited profit came from Sabine, Corpus, marketing or pipelines. The 2025 10-K does not allocate profit by train or business line. What it does report is $19.976 billion of revenue and $5.330 billion of net income attributable to Cheniere for the whole consolidated company. [2][4][5][12]

Let us walk a real customer through the system. In September 2026, Petrobras signed a 22-year SPA for approximately 0.8 million tonnes a year on an FOB basis. It is a long-duration procurement relationship, but there is no public price in the announcement. Cheniere's 10-K describes a general fixed-fee plus variable-fee structure for many long-term SPAs; the Petrobras release does not disclose whether or how that precise formula applies to this agreement. Petrobras describes the strategic purpose itself: contracted volumes can lower reliance on short-term purchases and give it more flexibility and security in meeting its contracts. It operates a receiving terminal at Guanabara Bay. The customer need is therefore not simply a molecule in isolation; it is predictable LNG supply that can enter the company's broader gas portfolio through import and regasification infrastructure. [2][3][13]

Behind that one cargo is a chain. Cheniere Marketing brings together the seller's contract, gas purchases and delivery planning. U.S. producers supply the feed gas; contracted pipeline capacity transports it from production basins to the Gulf Coast terminal. The liquefaction train removes impurities and cools the gas until it becomes a liquid. Tanks provide a buffer between production and a ship's arrival. Loading equipment moves the product onto a carrier. With the Petrobras FOB contract, the buyer takes delivery at the export terminal, provides the vessel and manages the voyage to Brazil. The receiving terminal warms the LNG back into gas before it reaches pipelines and end users. [2][3][4][5][13]

Now compare delivered-at-place. Cheniere can charter the ship and carry the cargo to the buyer's designated terminal. That is more than a different shipping invoice: it moves vessel scheduling, freight obligations and some execution exposure to the seller. The company has both kinds of commercial arrangements, plus short- and medium-term marketing sales and third-party LNG transactions. The deal-specific risk belongs to the contract, not to a generic statement about every cargo. [2]

You should also keep the accounting boundary in view. The filing says one customer did not reach ten percent of external-customer revenue in 2025, but one customer represented 15 percent of the combined trade receivables and contract assets balance at year-end. Revenue diversification and collection exposure are not the same test. Nor should you read a physical capacity number as a realized volume or contract value. Train availability, maintenance, weather, commissioning and customer delivery terms affect how much LNG is sold and when the related revenue is recorded. [2]

So when someone presents a breakdown of Cheniere into Sabine Pass, Corpus Christi and marketing, ask whether it is reported or modeled. Cheniere publishes detailed operating descriptions and project capacities, but it does not disclose those units as separate reportable segments. The honest answer is one integrated business, with no publicly reported facility-level revenue and profit mix. That limitation prevents a precise contribution ranking; it does not prevent you from tracing how the system works. [2][4][5]

The ownership chart adds another layer. Cheniere controls and consolidates Cheniere Partners, but held 48.6% of its limited-partner interests at year-end 2025. The parent also owned all of the general partner and incentive distribution rights. Outside investors therefore share in the controlled subsidiary's economics. The profit figure regularly presented to the CEO is net income attributable to Cheniere; consolidated net income and parent-attributable net income are not the same amount. Whenever you compare operating volume with shareholder earnings, keep that difference on the page. [2]

A common analytical error is to treat a facility fact as a segment fact. Sabine Pass processes more than 4.7 Bcf of gas per day and Corpus Christi expanded nominal capacity after Stage 3, but a capacity figure says nothing about exact revenue, contract margin or cash attributable to that facility. EIA's separate nominal and peak capacity definitions are another reminder that operational nameplate figures must be interpreted carefully. Stage 3 commissioning can add capacity before the full complex reaches a stable annual run rate. [4][5][6][10]

The commercial product also varies by handoff. Cheniere's FOB sale puts the buyer in charge of the vessel after terminal loading; a delivered sale makes Cheniere responsible for chartering and bringing the LNG to a specified receiving point. Those arrangements allocate freight, scheduling and destination decisions differently. Petrobras's agreement is clearly FOB. The public materials establish its term and quantity, while the exact price formula remains unavailable. That is an important positive finding of the research: the commercial example is concrete, but it does not authorize us to invent a confidential charge. [2][3][13]

A segment-level view also guards against confusing customer diversification with asset diversification. The 2025 filing says no one customer reached 10% of external-customer revenue, but a customer represented 15% of receivables and contract assets combined. Revenue may be spread across a wide buyer base while a particular balance remains concentrated. Likewise, two terminals reduce single-site operating dependence but both sit on the U.S. Gulf Coast and depend on reliable pipeline supply and export infrastructure. One segment does not mean one risk; it means management assesses a linked system. [2][4][5]

The 2026 Q3 release gives a useful example of what revenue disaggregation can and cannot tell you. LNG revenue was $6.099 billion; regasification revenue was $34 million; other revenue was $40 million; total revenue was $6.173 billion. Those rows identify revenue types, not the economics of separate reportable units. The filing does not tell you what net income, EBITDA or cash flow each category produced. Keep this period-specific revenue detail separate from the audited FY2025 segment facts. [2][3]

Distribution here is not a chain of stores or local dealers. Customers negotiate SPAs with Cheniere Marketing, and the affiliate coordinates contract volumes with physical LNG availability at the export plants. Long-term agreements can give a new train a customer before FID, while short-term arrangements can place uncontracted volumes or third-party cargoes. The channel is specialized and institutional, so credit evaluation, destination terms, cargo windows and shipping choices replace the retail acquisition metrics you might use for a consumer company. [2][3]

As you read the 10-K, separate the customer-country table from the plant map. Revenue geography is attributed to the principal place of business of the party to the agreement, while Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi identify where LNG is produced and loaded. A marketing transaction can span both. The country disclosure is useful for understanding the counterparty footprint, but it does not tell you which terminal supplied the cargo or which location produced the margin. [2]

QatarEnergy provides a second customer example, this time as future offtake rather than current output. The 2026 announcement says Cheniere affiliates signed up to 4 mtpa, FOB, for deliveries beginning in the early 2030s through 2054; one mtpa is conditional on the first phase of the Sabine Pass expansion reaching FID and other conditions. This agreement can help match new capacity with a buyer before construction, but the conditional quantity is not a train already built. The price is not disclosed, so you should not infer the economics from the duration alone. [3]

The segment note also explains the management view behind the disclosure choice. Cheniere's top executive receives consolidated results and the leadership team is functionally organized rather than by facility. Its one-segment reporting is consistent with an integrated service: procurement, transport, liquefaction, cargo marketing and delivery interact. That design can create operational efficiencies, but it makes an outside analyst's job harder. The right response is not to invent a plant-level earnings model and present it as reported fact; it is to mark the limit and analyze the consolidated cash system. [2]

The CODM's view is not a sign that facility-level operations are interchangeable. Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi have distinct permits, pipeline systems, train designs, marine access and expansion schedules. What the filing says is that Cheniere allocates resources and assesses performance across the consolidated business rather than presenting separate profit centers for those sites. You and I can analyze each physical project as an operating asset, while preserving the audited truth that the accounting segment remains one. [2][4][5]

This is also why country revenue is not a substitute for site economics. The accounting geography follows the customer's principal place of business, while Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi identify where LNG is produced and loaded. A marketing transaction can span both. You can describe a diverse global buyer base without claiming a certain share of Corpus Christi's trains serves Europe or that Sabine Pass earns a particular portion of net income. Those claims require disclosures Cheniere does not provide. [2]

book_subsections.title: Why a single segment is analytically useful
paragraphs: A single segment can reflect the way value is genuinely created. A terminal without feed gas, transportation, a contract and a vessel schedule cannot produce a customer delivery. Cheniere's organization treats those tasks as one integrated system. The cost of that integration is that outsiders receive less facility-level profit information. You can evaluate the consolidated cash engine and inspect operational milestones, but you cannot responsibly attribute a precise portion of earnings to each site. [2]

The customer example also reveals where responsibility changes hands. The FOB buyer takes delivery at the export terminal; the DAP seller arranges onward transport. Petrobras's agreement is FOB, and the public release states its term and annual quantity but not its price. That is enough to understand the route and the commercial risk allocation without pretending to know a confidential commercial term. [2][3][13]

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: You do not have to invent a segment split to understand a company. Here the better answer is that Cheniere sells an integrated LNG service, and the audited segment boundary follows that integrated operating model. The discipline is to connect the physical sites to the customer journey while leaving undisclosed facility economics undisclosed.
